Research gaps and challenges for initial scoping: The scoping process before starting a living review can be very rapid when using automation tools such as Trialstreamer, PubMed PICO Tool, or SWIFT-Review. These tools are useful for identifying the studies most likely to be relevant or higher-quality research with minimal user input. They cover a range of study types, from clinical trials to animal research and environmental toxicology studies. However, the caveat remains that these extremely rapid methods of scoping a research ﬁeld or reducing the amounts of studies needed to screen beforehand may produce incomplete or biased representa- tions of the evidence landscape. Reference retrieval Usually, reference retrieval involves experts, such as informa- tion specialists, searching multiple bibliographic databases up to a speciﬁc cut-off in time [23]. A living review requires periodic lit- erature searches and reference retrieval, thus increasing the work- load for information specialists in the absence of automation [1]. For the most basic living review workﬂow, a software tool should support identiﬁcation of new references to add to an ongo- ing project. New references need to be retrieved, merged, and de- duplicated against the existing dataset, to ensure that no refer- ences or studies already in use are deleted or overwritten. When done manually this usually involves multiple steps, using external reference-management software such as EndNote, and the process expends signiﬁcant resources if repeated on a daily, weekly, or monthly schedule for multiple data sources. Therefore, an opportu- nity for living review tools is to automate reference retrieval, de- duplication, and feeding new references into an existing screening workﬂow [3]. Tools: At the time of writing, four web-based applications with automated reference retrieval functionalities suitable for LSRs and other living review methodologies have emerged. NestedKnowl- edge is a new application; whereas DistillerSR, EPPI-Reviewer and SWIFT-ActiveScreener are applications that have integrated automatic reference retrieval as new features, as described on their websites and blogs (see Table 1 for sources). DistillerSR,2 NestedKnowledge,3 and SWIFT-ActiveScreener [24]4 are web-based collaborative applications to manage SR and evidence-mapping workﬂows. They all support PubMed as a data- base option for automatic searches, and can automatically pull refer- ences at regular intervals, based on a user-submitted systematic search strategy. In addition to PubMed, NestedKnowledge covers the Directory of Open Access Journals and ClinicalTrials.gov, Dis- tillerSR covers EBSCO, and SWIFT-ActiveScreener covers automatic imports from any Ovid-indexed materials for which users have insti- tutional access. None of these tools automate reference retrieval from pre-print servers. We found one other end-user tool that moved beyond the tra- ditional search-based approach to retrieving literature. EPPI- Reviewer [25]5 uses the OpenAlex citation graph [26] to update existing projects automatically with likely relevant references.6 However, some limitations persist when using automated refer- ence retrieval. Automation systems might not cover all important data sources, such that manual steps are necessary, particularly for de-duplication and management of records. As with all tools, trust in the reliability of the tools and evidence from published peer-reviewed literature of adequate performance are important considerations. Automatic reference deduplication algorithms have shown acceptable performance results [27], but inconsistent evaluation results remain across datasets and in the way their per- formance is assessed across the literature [27–29]. It is therefore important to consider screening tools without automation features that are compatible with living review workﬂows. They enable users to add references manually to ongoing projects, whilst still supporting multi-user collaborative web-environments. Some tools originally developed for traditional review workﬂows, such as Covidence7 or Abstrackr [30],8 do possess the functionality to update existing projects manually and are therefore still compatible with a living review workﬂow. Research gaps and challenges for reference retrieval: Automation tools are starting to integrate different data sources for automatic reference retrieval, to decrease recurring workloads for information specialists in living systematic or rapid reviews. However, tools currently tend to focus on speciﬁc data sources. Reviewers who wish to search multiple databases, clinical trial reg- istries or pre-print servers may still need to make compromises in methodology or update part of their evidence manually, depending on the number of databases that are available within their chosen review tool. When using end-user tools described in the earlier sections of this paper, users need to evaluate whether tools ﬁt their chosen liv- ing review methodology and data sources. They also need to famil- iarise themselves with the respective tool and verify it works as expected to build trust to the automated methods. None of the end-user tools mentioned above have published complete explana- tions and evaluations of their methods for automated reference retrieval and automatic deduplication and integration of data into ongoing living reviews. This remains one of the most important research evidence and information gaps. Screening Living reviews can yield large volumes of references that need to be screened for eligibility, depending on the topic of the research question. The mode of screening can vary. Human screening of all retrieved references on title/abstract and full-text level is the norm for SRs [23], often done in duplicate to avoid errors and to increase consistency. Rapid research methodologies such as evidence maps or rapid reviews may employ single-screening or screening on title/abstract-level only, at the author’s discretion. Many conven- tional SR tools now implement automation methods that re- order relevant references to the top, thus helping reviewers to ﬁnd relevant references faster. The next automation step is to consider stopping screening early on the basis that no further relevant ref- erences are likely to be missed. Tools: We previously mentioned DistillerSR, NestedKnowledge, Abstrackr, and EPPI-Reviewer. They are web-based collaborative end-user tools that include the functionality to screen references at title/abstract and full-text level and to apply tags, take notes, 2 https://v2dis-prod.evidencepartners.com/Login/Login.php (last accessed 08.03.2023) 3 https://nested-knowledge.com/ (last accessed 08.03.2023) 4 https://www.sciome.com/swift-activescreener/ (last accessed 08.03.2023) 5 https://eppi.ioe.ac.uk/CMS/Default.aspx?alias=eppi.ioe.ac.uk/cms/er4& (last accessed 08.03.2023) 6 https://eppi.ioe.ac.uk/cms/Default.aspx?tabid=3754 (last accessed 09.03.2023) 7 https://www.covidence.org/ (last accessed 08.03.2023) 8 http://abstrackr.cebm.brown.edu/account/login (last accessed 08.03.2023) L. and to capture data using hierarchical forms or questionnaires. They implement the principle of active learning for re-ordering ref- erences. This means that the tool uses human screening decisions on a project-by-project basis to train a machine-learning classiﬁer in the background, to move likely relevant references to the front of the screening pile while reviewers are actively working on the review. Crucially, active learning algorithms cannot replace one human reviewer or ‘take-over’ screening, rather their function is to manipulate the order of references with the aim to enable dis- covery of relevant references earlier on in the screening process. Beyond the traditional way of full duplicate screening of refer- ences, SWIFT-ActiveScreener has implemented active learning and an additional algorithm to estimate completeness of the screening in-process and to notify reviewers when they may stop manual screening early. Reviewers can decide to stop, for instance, when they are prompted that they reach a predicted 95 or 99% inclusion rate of likely relevant references. The actual number of references that can be omitted from screening will vary on a project-by-project basis, but on average 95% of all relevant refer- ences are found after screening 40% of the total [24]. Novel advances such as stopping screening early need to be well evaluated and reviewers should ensure that the data and charac- teristics of references used to evaluate such algorithms are repre- sentative of the data likely to appear within their reviews [24]. When applied correctly, active learning and early-stopping can add value especially for living evidence maps or living rapid reviews where it may be methodologically acceptable to avoid screening every single reference. In the context of a full LSR, such machine-learning and early-stopping algorithms can be useful to reduce weekly or monthly workload by screening only the likely relevant references regularly and introducing the opportunity to catch up screening the remainder at longer intervals. Research gaps and challenges for reference screening: There is no shortage of reference screening tools for literature reviews, in March 2023 the Systematic Review Toolbox alone listed 46 tools9 for this task. However, there are research gaps in the transparent and fair comparison of the performance of these tools, and the most recent systematic reviews addressing them are old or include rela- tively few of the available tools due to limitations such as limited availability and access due to licensing fees [9,31]. To provide accu- rate estimates of potential time-savings, large enough datasets with data from ﬁnished systematic reviews are needed [32]. Currently, a dataset with data from 24 reviews is available and has been used for the validation of several screening tools [24,33,34]. A larger data- set, as described by Muller et al. [32], would contribute towards solving current problems, such as evaluation of applicability of a tool or algorithm to different ﬁelds of literature review research. It would also facilitate inter-tool comparisons, by making evaluation results directly comparable. Data extraction and quality/bias-assessments Living reviews are long and work-intensive projects. For reviews in living mode, data extraction and quality assessment are either done continuously, or at pre-deﬁned intervals. Reviews that have a steady ﬂow of incoming included studies could there- fore beneﬁt from semi-automation of data extraction from the full text [1]. Tools: One included tool presented information speciﬁc to the semi-automation of this component of the workﬂow. RobotRe- viewer is an open-source web-based tool using traditional machine-learning and neural networks to extract data and to pre- dict risk of bias (RoB) for randomised controlled trials [12,17]. One previously discussed web-based search engine, Trial- streamer, is built on RobotReviewer’s methods. While other tools included in this review do support the manual extraction and appraisal of evidence, RobotReviewer, and Trialstreamer have gone furthest with the integration of automation and in making their tool and code accessible by using a transparent, well-reported, and open-source approach for validation [12,13]. One further RoB (semi)automation tool was published by Millard et al. [35], it is available as web-application to support the bias-assessment pro- cess.10 These are, to the best of our knowledge, the only end-user tools with automation for this task [10]. At the time of writing, a pilot case study about an upcoming, but not yet publicly released, software application called ‘RobotRe- viewer LIVE’ was published by Marshall et al. [17]. It is designed to combine RobotReviewer and Trialstreamer’s automation in a liv- ing review tool [17]. Research gaps and challenges for data extraction and quality/bias-assessments: In 2022, Jardim et al. conducted a user-centred, randomised study comparing human bias judge- ments with RobotReviewer and assessed acceptability of the sys- tem via group discussions and feedback. When replacing a human with RobotReviewer, they found that reviewers are as likely to be in consensus with the machine’s prediction as they are with assessments from other humans. They did however also ﬁnd that reviewers still preferred human-human interactions and that there is no signiﬁcant interest in integrating RobotReviewer’s automation into standard SR processes. To change the current per- ceptions on automated data extraction and RoB assessments they suggest that there need to be further quantiﬁcations of how much time can be saved using automation, and that more independent studies are needed to assess how RobotReviewer or other such (semi)automated systems perform in practice [36]. It was previously discussed by Thomas et al. [3] that automated data extraction and RoB may be used to replace one human reviewer, speciﬁcally in the context of living reviews. One practical application of this has materialised, via the of the usage of Trial- streamer in a case study of automatically mapping literature in real-time [20]. Synthesis Synthesising frequently updated reviews or reviews with many included studies is challenging. If a tool does not support the com- plete workﬂow needed for a speciﬁc project, then it is helpful to exchange data in a structured format that is compatible with other tools for downstream analysis [37]. We did not ﬁnd any accessible end-user tool with automation capacity for evidence synthesis, and discuss instead recent developments and ongoing research efforts related to the topic of synthesis and sharing data for synthesis between tools in the discussion section. Dissemination and visualisation of data In a living review project, research results are up-to-date, and as such they are most valuable when full or partial results are dissem- inated publicly as soon as possible or if they are otherwise made available to policymakers. This equally applies to LSRs and more rapid living review methodologies. The traditional peer-review system can be used to publish review updates, but it also intro- duces delays. Living review projects have therefore used custom- 9 http://systematicreviewtools.com/software.php (last accessed 08.03.2023) 10 http://www.datamining.org.uk/sysreview.html (last accessed 19.06.2023) 70 L. built solutions such as interactive dashboards or websites to share the status quo of their living evidence. This is shown for example by the COVID NMA project, sharing visualisations that summarise extracted data.11 The usage of pre-print servers has emerged as a potential solution for authors of living reviews. It is becoming an acceptable option for an increasing number of journals and publish- ers, to bridge the time-gap between manuscript submission and publication and to alleviate pressure on journals and peer- reviewers to process articles expeditiously. Journals and publishing groups such as the BMJ, Frontiers, or PLOS already encourage pre- prints with MedRxiv12 while the Lancet Group maintains its own dedicated pre-print servers for afﬁliated journals.13 Pre-print servers are therefore very useful platforms for authors of living reviews not only to discover the latest research related to their review, but also to disseminate their own research, once their living reviews have reached a publishable format. However, the core-challenges pertaining to the use of pre-print servers are faced not by the authors, but rather by the audience of the literature. Readers of articles from pre-print servers will need to be aware that a pre-print may not follow high standards in terms of clarity, quality of reporting or availability of data, due to a lack of quality-control from an established publisher [6,38]. Tools: We found two tools that speciﬁcally focus on the dissem- ination of living evidence. MAGICapp is a web-application for guidelines developers. The platform support living guidelines and disseminates results directly through the application. The MAGI- Capp platform includes an API to connect with SR software such as EPPI-reviewer that can be used to manage various components of the review workﬂow.14 The second tool included for evidence dis- semination is EPPI-Mapper, a living evidence-mapping tool afﬁliated with EPPI-Reviewer. EPPI-Mapper is a web-application for interac- tively querying and visualizing evidence maps, or sharing living review results in real-time. Projects are publicly accessible and data can be ﬁltered by tags and date.15 During the past two years project-speciﬁc dashboards inte- grated with review software to show review data, such as the EPPI-Mapper project for evidence maps or the MAGICApp, have emerged. The usage of such dedicated software to make results accessible brings reviews to life because continuous accessibility/ usage of data is a good justiﬁcation for continuous evidence updates. Similarly important, the ability to show results and to produce research outputs on a rolling and automated basis acts as motivation for reviewers, without which it may be challenging to ﬁnd the necessary motivation to keep the project ‘alive’. We also found tools to automate or streamline the process of creating single visualisations that can be shared to communicate progress made within living review projects. Study ﬂow diagrams, for example, are useful for visualising progress and development of the evidence between review updates [39]. In general, a PRISMA diagram can be manually created. However, to save time, the PRISMA202016 web application allows users to manually ﬁll in a form or to upload a CSV ﬁle to create the diagram, based on the latest PRISMA2020 statement [40]. Its open-source nature and availability as R package allows integration with other tools. NestedKnowledge, DistillerSR and SWIFT-ActiveScreener also support automated PRISMA diagrams with functionality to re- create the diagrams as living reviews get updated. NestedKnowl- edge furthermore allows manual manuscript drafting within the software, similar to the way how reviewers can do write-up within Cochrane’s ReviewManager software. Through logging of user deci- sions, DistillerSR makes reviews audit-compatible through auto- matic reports. SWIFT-ActiveScreener, similar to DistillerSR, monitors progress, contributions per screener, screener- and data extraction conﬂicts, and make these data available as reports. Research gaps and practical challenges for dissemination and visualisation of data: Disseminating research data and ﬁnd- ings can be challenging for both practical and legal reasons. For legal reasons, publicly sharing raw data, such as included abstracts or RIS ﬁles with included references can violate pub- lisher’s copyrights. Sharing before publication can also foster unau- thorized or uncredited use of research data, which may deter researchers from sharing results in real-time. At the same time a living project might value speed over consistency of extracted data, with quality checks not being the top priority. In this case the reviewers would consider restricting the data that is publicly shared until full quality assessment can take place. Some of these problems can be addressed by software that provides read-only online dashboards or by sharing visualisations such as PRISMA dia- grams that only give overviews of the number of included studies or the number of studies that were data-extracted or categorised for any given topic. Other resources and platforms Thomas et al. [3] discuss ‘Citizen Science’ and the opportunity of outsourcing part of a living review’s workload to the crowd. To enable this, platforms are needed to connect author teams with students, other researchers, or with interested citizens. In their paper, Thomas et al. [3] describe opportunities for breaking down living review processes into smaller and clearly-deﬁned ‘micro- tasks’ and enlisting help of many volunteers, with the aim of increasing overall speed and efﬁciency gains in the living-review- process [3]. We included two crowd-sourcing platforms that can be helpful to alleviate the burden for LSRs or other living review projects, and thus help to make them feasible and to keep them ‘alive’. The Cochrane TaskExchange17 and the CrowdCARE [41]18 platforms were identiﬁed and included in this narrative review because they offer the possibility to coordinate and to expedite living review processes by outsourcing work during various parts of the workﬂow. Cochrane TaskExchange is a platform where any type of work relevant to SRs can be advertised for crowd-sourcing and where authors can manage the process of enlisting crowd- members for their projects. CrowdCARE is more speciﬁc in its aims, as it focuses on crowd-sourcing one of the most time-intensive review microtasks: assessment of study quality [41]. While crowd- sourcing does ease the workload, reviewers should still be careful to check for consistency and to ensure that data are high-quality. Although we did not include guidelines and tools for quality assessment in this discussion, we found two publications that are potentially useful for authors of living reviews to guide them through the decision-making process of when to publish full review updates [42,43]. We did not identify any software tools that automatically alert authors to publish full updates, but we did identify the guidance documents and checklists that discuss SR updates, with applicabil- ity to living evidence [42,43].19 Discussion This narrative review aimed to provide an overview of current automation and software tools that help review authors to proceed with optimal efﬁciency when conducting any kind of living evi- dence synthesis. We included 11 end-user tools that address seven common workﬂow steps when conducting and maintaining living reviews. For each workﬂow step, we examined features offered by the tools that could support living evidence projects, including manual, semi-automated, and fully automated approaches to sup- port LSRs, living rapid reviews or evidence maps. To our knowledge this is the ﬁrst review focussing on living review tools. Practical challenges No tool covered the whole living review workﬂow while at the same time providing a complete, transparent, and published valida- tion of their automation methods. This suggests that there exist challenges from the perspective of software developers in designing and publishing such end-user tools. To highlight potential issues for living-review tool development we introduce a case study of devel- oping and using a living review web-application tailored to a speci- ﬁc LSR, described in Figure 2. We developed it for a living review of the impact of COVID-19 on self-harm and suicidal behaviour, with daily monitoring of evidence between May 2020 and August 2022. In 2020 there were no existing tools to (semi-)automate this workﬂow, which necessitated building a custom web-framework to manage the LSR. It covers the workﬂow steps of reference retrieval, screening, data extraction, and visualisation with varying degrees of automation. The tool is available as open-source code repository and requires local deployment and set up,20 and thus does not qual- ify as an end-user tool in the context of this paper. Research gaps for living review automation The two biggest gaps in automation features were found in grouping related references referring to the same study cohorts, and in general coverage of evidence synthesis. Identifying published versions of pre-prints or other publica- tions of studies was a time-consuming, manual challenge during our case study. Published methods exist, for example, to identify published articles from records included in clinical trial registries [44,45]. Smalheiser and Holt [46] describe a web-application to Figure 2. To enhance automation in living reviews, such func- tionalities could be expanded to include pre-print linking and to ease integration with downstream SR tools. Integration between tools to facilitate synthesis of data is the second research gap. Every review topic is unique, and different kinds of review methodologies (systematic, rapid, mapping) can be living and thus require different work for synthesis. For exam- ple, including the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 tool within a tool’s sup- ported workﬂow would enable integrated discussion and assessments of RoB for randomised controlled trials but would not cover non-randomised study designs. In this case it is helpful if extracted data can be imported or exported in a straightforward manner between different tools for synthesis. Common non- proprietary and freely accessible export formats across tools are RIS for references and CSV for data. These are simpliﬁed ways of making data accessible for reference management or statistical analysis with more specialised software. To facilitate this, standards for interoperability and data exchange between tools are needed, not only for living reviews but also for automation of literature reviews in general. Current research efforts addressing this issue are focusing on the develop- ment of complex interoperability standards such as the FHIR Resources for Evidence-Based Medicine Knowledge Assets, also known as EBMonFHIR [47], or an ongoing effort called C-TrO, to describe clinical trial data in ontology-format and to develop web-based tools for sharing and analysis to support automation in this workﬂow component [48,49]. Limitations The selection of tools discussed in this narrative review is lim- ited to tools supporting, automating, or ﬁnding novel approaches to living review workﬂow steps. It is therefore not a complete over- view of the status quo of systematic review automation, and does not fully cover tools or features of some tools that are tailored to support traditional, ‘static’ reviews. In general, all of the included tools can be used for standard systematic or rapid reviews, because the ‘living’ component of an evidence synthesis focuses on revised updating strategies of evidence within a review and it does not change review methodologies overall. Not all tools includeed in this narrative review are associated with up-to-date peer- reviewed publications, and there are therefore instances where no ofﬁcial, transparent validation of some features of a tool is avail- able. We provide a discussion of automation features as they are described by tool developers and include supplementary ‘soft’ sources of information such as ofﬁcial websites and blogs belong- ing to each tool. This serves to increase the chance of discovering up-to-date living review features for each tool, even if the quality of such sources is generally considered to be lower than peer- reviewed publications. We discuss caveats and challenges relating to using these tools, since automation methods are not always fully described and not all evaluations done by tool providers are pub- lished transparently. Conclusion Living reviews can evolve in parallel with the evidence that is generated for a given topic, if all processes within the workﬂow are sufﬁciently ﬂexible to adapt to changing needs and are reported in a transparent manner. There are several ways to make living reviews more feasible, most (but not all) focusing on automation and efﬁciency of the review process. The use of dedi- cated staff or crowd resources, development of automated update and monitoring systems, and the use of simpliﬁcation and stan- dardized methods are just some approaches that may help to speed up processes. Pre-prints or dedicated web-presences for automatic dissemination of in-progress evidence updates, rather than solely relying on peer-reviewed journal publications, are important to make the effort of undertaking living evidence synthesis a worthwhile endeavour. Despite offering basic living review func- tionalities, the RobotReviewer tool family and the four existing end-user tools (NestedKnowledge, SWIFT-ActiveScreener, Dis- tillerSR, EPPI-Reviewer) that cover most of the workﬂow should still be further developed. Areas with research potential are broader evidence retrieval from different data sources, integrating automation beyond active-learning for screening, grouping multi- ple papers based on the same cohort of patients (or follow-up pub- lications) under a single study, pre-print matching, and ensuring interoperability using clearly deﬁned data-exchange standards to facilitate the creation of data sharing and dissemination pipelines. Smart Learning Environments           (2023) 10:15 Smart Learning Environments What if the devil is my guardian angel: ChatGPT as a case study of using chatbots in education Ahmed Tlili1   , Boulus Shehata1   , Michael Agyemang Adarkwah1*   , Aras Bozkurt2   , Daniel T. Hickey3   , Ronghuai Huang1    and Brighter Agyemang4 Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies have been progressing constantly and being more visible in different aspects of our lives. One recent phenomenon is ChatGPT, a chatbot with a conversational artificial intelligence interface that was developed by OpenAI. As one of the most advanced artificial intelligence applications, ChatGPT has drawn much public attention across the globe. In this regard, this study examines ChatGPT in education, among early adopters, through a qualitative instrumental case study. Conducted in three stages, the first stage of the study reveals that the public discourse in social media is generally positive and there is enthusiasm regarding its use in educational settings. However, there are also voices who are approaching cautiously using ChatGPT in educational settings. The second stage of the study examines the case of ChatGPT through lenses of educational transformation, response quality, useful- ness, personality and emotion, and ethics. In the third and final stage of the study, the investigation of user experiences through ten educational scenarios revealed various issues, including cheating, honesty and truthfulness of ChatGPT, privacy misleading, and manipulation. The findings of this study provide several research directions that should be considered to ensure a safe and responsible adoption of chatbots, specifi- cally ChatGPT, in education. Keywords:  Generative AI, ChatGPT, Chatbots, Education, Artificial intelligence, Human–machine collaboration Introduction Can machines think? is a simple, yet a sophisticated question (Turing, 1950). In an effort to find an answer to this question, McCarthy et al. (1955) organized a scholarly event and coined the term "artificial intelligence” (AI) in 1955 to refer to machines and pro- cesses that imitate human cognition and make decisions like humans. At these times, the term [ro]bots are articulated for the first time in Čapek’s (1921) science fiction play; however, it was Asimov (1942, 1950) who visioned that these machines can transform into intelligent forms and introduced the Three Laws of Robotics to set the rules that bots should stick to and cannot be bypassed. Smart Learning Environments           (2023) 10:15 the Turing Test was proposed as a code of protocol to understand whether a machine can exhibit intelligent behavior equivalent to, or indistinguishable from, that of a human (Turing, 1950). Once depicted as fiction, all those possibilities are about to come true, and we are at the brink of a future when we can know whether machines can think or not. In November 2022, OpenAI, a lab that studies artificial intelligence, came out with a chatbot called ChatGPT (Generative Pre-trained Transformer). ChatGPT is a conversa- tional artificial intelligence interface that uses natural language processing (NLP), which interacts in a realistic way and even “answers follow-up questions, admits its mistakes, challenges incorrect premises, and rejects inappropriate requests’’ (OpenAI, 2023). While ChatGPT’s primary function was to mimic human conversation, its capabilities extend far beyond that; it can literally create new things, such as a poem, story, or novel, or act like anything within its capability. With the advent of ChatGPT, there is eventually an innovative AI technology that will truly challenge the Turing Test (Turing, 1950) and demonstrate if it is capable of think- ing like humans. It is uncertain if it would pass the Turing Test (Turing, 1950) in the long run, but it is sure that ChatGPT is revolutionary as a conversational AI-powered bot, and it is a visible signal for the paradigm shift that has been happening not only in the educational landscape, but also in every dimension of our lives. Compared to traditional chatbots, ChatGPT is based on GPT-3, which is the third iteration of the GPT series by OpenAI that is more advanced in terms of scale (175 billion parameters, compared to 1.5 billion of GPT-2), larger dataset as the training data, more fine-tuning, enhanced capabilities, and more human-like text generations (Brown et al., 2020). The use of Natu- ral Language Processing and a generative AI that relies on deep learning has enabled ChatGPT to produce human-like text and maintain a conversational style allowing more realistic natural dialogues. Several preprints of studies and numerous blog posts and media outlets have reported the advantages of ChatGPT in education (Zhai, 2022); some have even provided guide- lines on using it in classrooms (Lieberman, 2023; Mollick & Mollick, 2022; Ofgang, 2022). However, the potential concerns of chatbots haven’t been investigated as much. Janssen et al. (2021) described reasons for chatbots’ failure in practice, including not hav- ing enough resources, wrong use case (i.e., the basic chatbot technology did not match the required task), poor law regulations, data security, and liability concerns, ignorance of user expectation and bad conversation design, or simply poor content. Haque et al. (2022) did a Twitter sentiment analysis about ChatGPT adoption as a technology in general (not in education), and they found that users have divided attitudes about it. However, concerns coming from an advanced chatbot, such as ChatGPT, were not well investigated in the education field. Therefore, it is not clear if ChatGPT will overcome the concerns found in previous chatbots or will even deepen them. Consequently, this may lead to a serious and quick protective reaction to a potential opportunity, such as New York City and Los Angeles Unified schools’ banning of ChatGPT from educational networks due to the risk of using it to cheat in assignments (Shen-Berro, 2023; The Guardian, 2023). It is therefore important to investigate the concerns of using this tech- nology, ChatGPT, in education to ensure safe use. The purpose of this study is, therefore, to examine chatbots in education and for this purpose, the study approaches ChatGPT

as a representative case of an advanced chatbot among early adopters. In this regard, this study answers the following research question: What are the concerns of using chatbots, specifically ChatGPT, in education? Methodology To answer the aforementioned research question, this study adopts a qualitative case study approach (Yin, 1984) and benefits from an instrumental case study research design (Stake, 1995). Instrumental research design is helpful when researchers intend to under- stand a phenomenon in a context (Stake, 1995), which is in our case, ChatGPT which is a fine and recent example of AI-powered chatbots. To ensure the validity and reliabil- ity of the study, the research triangulates (Thurmond, 2001) the data collection tools to get a broader and deeper understanding. In this regard, this study follows three stages, namely, social network analysis of tweets, content analysis of interviews, and investiga- tion of user experiences. Each of the stages is described in the next subsequent sections. Social network analysis of tweets Tweet analysis aims to understand the public discourse on the use of ChatGPT in edu- cation. Specifically, a cross-sectional analysis of tweets was conducted through Social Network Analysis (SNA) (Hansen et al., 2010). Specifically, from December 23, 2022, to January 6, 2023, 2330 tweets, from 1530 Twitter users, were collected and analyzed con- taining the following search string: “#ChatGPT* AND (education OR teaching OR learn- ing)”. The dataset was compiled through social network analysis (Hansen et al., 2010) and the content of the tweets was further examined through sentiment analysis (Giacha- nou & Crestani, 2016) and tSNE analysis (van der Maaten & Hinton, 2008). Content analysis of interviews Interview analysis was conducted to investigate how different stakeholders (students, educators, etc.) perceive the use of ChatGPT in education, especially the concerns they have about it. Specifically, 19 interviewees, who have been using ChatGPT in education and posting their experiences through blogs publicly, were recruited from their chan- nels. The interviewer had a long experience of using chatbots in education, and specifi- cally had been using ChatGPT for at least one month. For the interviewees, despite that they were carefully chosen for this study to ensure the reliability of the findings, we fur- ther asked them to rate their familiarity with Chatbots, on a scale from 1 to 5 (where 1 is not familiar and 5 is very familiar). The interviews had an average of 3.02 related to the familiarity with chatbots, which reflect their appropriateness for this study. The inter- viewees were selected with various working backgrounds, such as educators, developers, students, and AI freelancers, to ensure the solicitation of rich answers from each one’s perspective. To analyse the collected interviews, content analysis, which is one of the classical procedures for analysing textual materials, was used (Flick, 2009). The analysis was based on the steps proposed by Erlingsson and Brysiewicz (2017). Particularly, two coders read the given interview results before they start coding them based on the devel- oped coding scheme in Table 1.

Smart Learning Environments           (2023) 10:15 Investigation of user experiences User experience aims to conduct hands-on experiences of using ChatGPT and iden- tify potential concerns that might be faced when using it in education. User experience involves human perceptions and responses that result from the use of a product, sys- tem, or service. User Experience points to a more global projective goal: not just attain effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction, but it aims to enhance the entire experience of the user, from the expectation, through interaction and finally the reflection about the experience (Beccari & Oliveira, 2011). In this context, three experienced educators have used ChatGPT for a whole week to test similar and different teaching/learning scenar- ios, and then see the obtained results accordingly. In this context, daily meetings during the whole week were conducted between these educators to discuss and summarize the obtained results. Results The obtained results were structured according to each stage as discussed in the follow- ing subsequent sections. Social network analysis of tweets The overall aim of social network analysis is to learn more about public discourse regard- ing the use of ChatGPT from the perspective of educational purposes. Figure 1 shows tweets analysis using the Harel-Koren Fast Multiscale algorithm, which is a fast multi- level graph layout that provides better visualizations (Harel & Koren, 2001). Specifically, the edge colors, opacities, and widths are based on edge weight values. The node sizes are based on betweenness centrality values. Each interaction (e.g., retweets, mentions, likes) is identified as a relation and visualized as an edge. While some of the sub-clusters demonstrate that some participants gathered around some ideas, the overall network is composed of isolated nodes (e.g., see the largest cluster on the upper left side of Fig. 1). Accordingly, Fig. 1 shows a fragmented brand cluster pattern (Rainie, 2014; Smith et al., 2014) implying that the community formation about ChatGPT is fragmented, and indi- viduals are seeking more information and discussion about its limitations and promises by tethering some influencer nodes in the ChatGPT network. The most used word pairs also provide interesting insights. For instance, some sug- gest how to use AI-powered ChatGPT (e.g., education—chatgpt, education—learn- ing, focused—grading, etc.), and some others hint that educational systems are in a Table 1  Definition of codes Code Definition Educational transformation Use this code when users are talking about how ChatGPT will change education Response quality Use this code when users are talking about the accuracy of the obtained results from ChatGPT Usefulness Use this code when users are talking about how ChatGPT helped them in educa- tion Personality and emotion Use this code when users are talking about their feelings when interacting with ChatGPT or if mentioning the emotions revealed by ChatGPT Ethics Use this code when users are talking about the ethical concerns of using ChatGPT in education

turning point (e.g., existential—crisis, kind—ironic, crisis—happening, forgotten— purpose, etc.). The general public’s view on the use of chatbots, more specifically ChatGPT, is diverse and there is no collective consensus on whether it is a hype or a future opportunity. However, the sentiment analysis of tweets (Giachanou & Crestani, 2016), demonstrates that the positive sentiments (5%) outweigh the negative senti- ments (2.5%) (see Table 2). The fact that non-categorized sentiments (92.5%) are in the majority can be considered as an indicator that most people are undecided about ChatGPT in education. The positive and negative sentiments are clearly reflected in some tweets with high edge weight values (Hansen et al., 2010). An example of positive sentiments is: •	 As a language model trained by OpenAI, I’m constantly amazed by the power & potential of artificial intelligence. From natural language processing to machine learning, AI is revolutionizing the way we think about & interact with technology.

An example of negative sentiments is: •	 Here’s my problem with this line of thinking about #ChatGPT as a writing instruc- tor. Reactionary teaching goes nowhere. As seen in the sample tweets (see Table 3), despite that there is an optimistic overview of using ChatGPT in education, there are also some concerns regarding the use of such technologies in the educational landscape. To summarize, the findings from the Social Network Analysis of tweets revealed that positive sentiments have shown almost as twice higher frequency than negative ones (see Table 2). However, the example tweets show that negative sentiments demonstrate deeper and critical thinking than the positive ones (see Table 3). This could be explained by the fact that most of the positive sentiments are led by the novelty effect of Chat- GPT as a technology in education.
