Context window memory is one of the most commonly used methods (Zhang et al., 2023; Pang et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024c; Qu et al., 2024; Ning and Liu, 2024; Xie et al., 2024; Kannan et al., 2024a; Song et al., 2023; Jo et al., 2023; Boiko et al., 2023; Goodell et al., 2025). Using the internal mechanisms of the transformer, it retains recent inputs and preserves local coherence throughout the prompt. This approach enables agents to main­ tain consistency during short interactions without relying on external systems. In contrast, conversational and dialogue history stores complete sequences of past interactions to sup­ port context-aware responses and maintain continuity over extended sessions (Wang et al., 2024d; Li et al., 2023a; Jo et al., 2023; Wei et al., 2024; Ghafarollahi and Buehler, 2024; Barra et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025c). More complex memory implementations include Reflexion-style memory systems, which integrate recent context with structured representations of prior outcomes, allowing agents to update behavior based on previous successes and failures (Singh et al., 2024; Feng et al., 2024; Shinn et al., 2023; Bo et al., 2024). Furthermore, RAG methods connect agents to external knowledge sources during inference, enabling access to factual information (Wang et al., 2025b; Jin et al., 2024; Barra et al., 2025; Goodell et al., 2025). The components of the working memory and the scratchpad temporarily hold intermediate reasoning steps and enable sequential problem solving (Abdaljalil et al., 2025; Cai et al., 2025). In parallel, long-term episodic memory models iteratively capture and organize agent experiences, sup­ porting generalization of past situations and improving task adaptation (Zhang et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2024d). Specific systems apply short-term memory optimization techniques for immediate reactivity tasks to focus on rapid access to updated data while minimizing over­ head (Bo et al., 2024; Jo et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2024). Several systems implement hybrid memory mechanisms, including models that merge local prompt-based memory with persistent indexed documents (Boiko et al., 2023). These designs reflect ongo­ ing efforts to construct memory architectures that support immediate responsiveness and long-term behavioral consistency. Different memory mechanisms vary in effectiveness according to the task and the context of the agent. Context window memory suits short-term, reactive tasks, while conversational and episodic memory support extended interactions and continuity. Retrieval-augmented and hybrid systems improve access to external knowledge, enhancing reasoning in complex domains. In multi-agent settings, structured and dynamic memory enable coordinated plan­ ning. In general, memory designs are most effective when aligned with specific operational demands. 8  Impact of prompting, fine-tuning, and memory augmentation Although foundational LLMs have extensive general knowledge and strong reasoning skills, they are not automatically independent agents. Unlike parametric approaches like fine-tuning, which change a model’s weights, prompt engineering works during inference time. It offers a simple way to define tasks, assign roles, and control agent behavior dynamically without needing a lot of computing power. This method takes advan­ tage of the natural instruction-following and in-context learning abilities of LLMs to man­ age complex tasks (Abdaljalil et al., 2025). The flexibility of prompting makes it the primary way to set goals, integrate tools, and simulate complex social interactions. At the single-agent level, prompt engineering plays a key role in defin­ ing an agent’s operational settings and reasoning style. For instance, Reflexion (Shinn et al., 2023) demonstrates how prompts enable self-reflection without weight updates, achieving performance improvements through feedback-guided adjustments. This type of self-correc­ tion, guided by prompts, also works well in dynamic situations. (Behari et al., 2024) used a Decision-Language Model (DLM) to understand natural language policy goals, suggest reward functions as code, and adjust them based on the results of simulations. Moreover, fine-tuning introduces risks, including model overfitting, amplification of biases present in the training data, and susceptibility to malicious data injection. While fine- tuning can achieve higher task-specific performance, it requires careful dataset curation, extensive computational resources, and rigorous validation. In contrast, prompt engineering offers flexibility and safety, but generally cannot reach the same depth of expertise. 8.3  Memory augmentation: enabling grounded reasoning and experiential learning While prompting gives immediate instructions for an agent, memory augmentation extends agents beyond context limits (Lu et al., 2024; Jin et al., 2024) by changing them from simple instruction-followers into adaptable systems (Jin and Ma, 2024). Memory can be divided into two main types: retrieval of external knowledge (RAG) and accumulation of internal dynamic experience that supports learning and self-correction. RAG grounds agent reason­ ing in verifiable information. It helps reduce mistakes and improve reliability. For example, in clinical settings, frameworks like TRIAGEAGENT (Lu et al., 2024) and ColaCare (Wang et al., 2025b) use RAG to give agents access to medical handbooks and guidelines. This ensures their decisions are based on solid evidence. This method works well in specialized technical areas; (Barra et al., 2025) employs RAG to offer established simulation guide­ lines for scenario design. Xia et al. (2024) use it to access technical datasheets for creating digital twin models. However, the effectiveness of RAG can depend on the model. Xia et al. mention a “cheat-sheet effect,” where it greatly improves performance in weaker LLMs compared to stronger ones. This suggests that the value of external memory depends on the agent’s inherent reasoning capabilities. The external memory can also be dynamic, as shown in frameworks like DeCoAgent (Jin et al., 2024). Here, a JSON memory module pulls cur­ rent on-chain data, preventing unnecessary blockchain scans. Beyond retrieving static facts, memory is vital for experiential and reflective learning. One important framework in this area is Reflexion (Shinn et al., 2023) that stores verbal reflections in episodic buffers. This helps guide future attempts. This process of self-correction has been shown to be effective in many applications, from improving public health policies in simulations (Behari et al., 2024) to generating high-quality distillation data for training other models (Yang et al., 2024d). However, compared to an episodic system like Reflexion, RAG is more reliable for factual grounding but less effective for long-term adaptation. The concept has evolved into more organized, long-lasting memory systems. REMEMBERER (Zhang et al., 2023) updates an agent’s long-term experience memory through RL. AVATAR (Wu et al., 2024) maintains a "Memory Bank" to store high-performing action sequences and instructions. Similarly, Star-Agents (Zhou et al., 2024) uses an "Instruction Memory Bank" to continu­ ously improve data generation strategies. Memory also helps agents stay grounded in their immediate, dynamic environment, especially in interactive settings. This is often done by updating the agent’s prompt with real-time perceptual information. For example, Song et al. (2023) keep plans grounded in LLM-Planner by constantly updating the prompt with a list of visually perceived objects. Yang et al. (2024c) use prompts to coordinate visual ground­ ing tools. This grounding includes more abstract representations of the state as well. Li et al. 1 3 71

In multi-agent systems, memory can be distributed. The CoA framework from Zhang et al. (2024c) passes a "Communication Unit" in sequence between agents, allowing each to build on the previous work. A more complex version is CoELA (Zhang et al., 2024d), which resembles human thinking with dis­ tinct semantic, episodic, and procedural memory modules to support long-term cooperation. Despite its advantages, memory enhancement is not perfect and faces significant challenges. The main limitation lies in how well the agent can manage long and complex memory streams. George et al. (2024) points out that even with CoT prompting, agents can struggle to use crucial information from lengthy histories filled with distracting facts. Additionally, some memory strategies can backfire in specific situations. Zhang et al. (2024e) discovered that a Reflexion-style memory system led to worse performance in complex multitasking scenarios. Sometimes, simpler approaches like a "sliding window" memory can be a more effective, if less advanced, solution (Chang et al., 2024). Ultimately, how well memory is implemented is what distinguishes an agent as a reactive tool versus a cognitive entity capable of learning, adapting, and maintaining coherent long-term behavior. 8.4  The synergistic integration of prompting, fine-tuning, and memory The development of capable LLM-based agents relies on the interaction of prompting, fine- tuning, and memory augmentation (Ni and Buehler, 2024; Cheng et al., 2024b; Zhang et al., 2024e). The combined use of these three elements is crucial for increasing agent autonomy, from single-agent reasoning to complex multi-agent collaboration (Kim et al., 2024; Ni and Buehler, 2024; Ghafarollahi and Buehler, 2024). At its core, prompt engineering is the main method for guiding agent behavior. However, relying solely on prompting can be fragile. Performance drops significantly when agents deal with long contexts filled with distracting "red herring" facts, even with CoT prompting. While prompting provides dynamic control, fine-tuning offers a method for permanently embedding specialized knowledge and complex skills in an agent. This is essential for creating agents that are trained by instructions and are inherently capable in specific domains. One of the most effective combinations occurs when prompting serves as a tool for generating data, creating high-quality datasets for refining smaller, more efficient agents. This model allows the reasoning abilities of large propri­ etary models to be distilled into open-source alternatives. A clear example is the ToolLLM framework (Qin et al., 2024), which uses ChatGPT to produce a vast dataset of instructions and API call solutions to fine-tune LLaMA into the highly effective ToolLLaMA. A similar method is used by Qian et al. (2024) to develop Mistral-Interact by fine-tuning on user dialogues generated by prompting GPT-4. Pang et al. (2024) also use the MATRIX frame­ work to create alignment data. This bidirectional relationship extends further: fine-tuning can enhance an agent’s ability to follow complex prompts and execute domain-specific instructions more reliably. Yin et al. (2024) demonstrate this with the LUMOS framework, showing that fine-tuning on unified, high-quality annotations improves both planning and grounding abilities when combined with structured prompting strategies. Memory augmentation bridges prompting and fine-tuning mechanisms by providing the contextual foundation necessary for effective prompting and the experiential data required for targeted fine-tuning. RAG-based systems like TRIAGEAGENT (Lu et al., 2024) and ColaCare (Wang et al., 2025b) use external memory to ground prompts in factual medical 1 3 71

Conversely, episodic memory sys­ tems like Reflexion (Shinn et al., 2023) accumulate task-specific experience in the form of episodic verbal reflections, which are used in subsequent prompts to improve both immedi­ ate reasoning and performance. The most advanced agents successfully combine all three components. In these systems, fine-tuning develops core skills, prompting guides inference- time reasoning and tool use, while memory offers dynamic context and knowledge. The CoELA framework (Zhang et al., 2024d) fine-tunes CoLLAMA using data collected by agents and applies structured prompts alongside a multi-part memory system (semantic, episodic, procedural) to enable complex collaboration. OmniJARVIS (Wang et al., 2024c) demonstrates this integration by fine-tuning a VLA model on unified tokens that represent instructions, memories, and actions. These tokens are coordinated by prompts for open- world tasks. These systems illustrate that, while each mechanism is effective independently, their combination is essential for developing truly autonomous, capable, and reliable LLM- based agents. 9  Evaluation benchmarks and datasets The rapid growth of LLM agents has required a change in how we evaluate them. Early methods that depended on static NLP benchmarks do not effectively capture the interactive, goal-driven, and often multi-step nature of these systems. The literature shows a clear shift towards more dynamic, specific, and analytical evaluation methods (Zhang et al., 2024e; Wijk et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2024d). To give a clear overview of this progress, this section looks at the evaluation landscape through three connected lenses. First, it reviews the specialized benchmarks and interactive environments designed to test the abilities of agents in realistic situations (Chang et al., 2024; Lu et al., 2024). Next, it examines the various methods and metrics developed to judge performance beyond simple accuracy, including factors like efficiency, quality, and behavioral strength (Chang et al., 2024). Finally, the section highlights the important role of the datasets used to train and ground these agents since they provide the basis for agentic behavior. 9.1  Task-oriented and interactive benchmarks Evaluating the capabilities of LLM-based agents requires a shift from static language met­ rics to dynamic benchmarks that focus on task performance and interactivity in complex environments. A notable trend is the creation of simulated environments where agents must engage in multi-step reasoning and actions. For example, TIME-ARENA (Zhang et al., 2024e) introduced a text-based simulation that includes time-based dynamics and con­ straints, challenging agents with multitasking scenarios in cooking, household tasks, and lab work. Advancing this complexity, AndroidArena (Xing et al., 2024) offers a general- purpose operating system environment to assess agents on intricate tasks that need coopera­ tion between applications and compliance with user constraints. In a more specific area, RE-Bench provides demanding, open-ended machine learning research tasks, allowing for a direct comparison between AI agents and human experts. Environments like Overcooked- AI, ALFRED, and WebShop are established settings for testing zero-shot coordination, 1 3 71

An important part of agent functionality is their ability to interact with and manipulate external tools and APIs. ToolLLM introduced ToolBench, which is a detailed instruction- tuning dataset with over 16,000 real-world APIs, along with an automatic evaluator called ToolEval to assess pass rates and solution quality (Qin et  al., 2024). Frameworks like EASYTOOL aim to improve agent performance on these benchmarks by converting exten­ sive tool documentation into brief, clear instructions (Yuan et al., 2025). The assessment of tool use also includes specialized scientific fields. For instance, ChemCrow and Coscientist are agent systems evaluated on their ability to plan and carry out complex chemical synthe­ ses using expert-designed chemistry tools (Bran et al., 2024; Boiko et al., 2023). In indus­ trial applications, RCAgent showcases a tool-enhanced agent for cloud root cause analysis, evaluated using proprietary system log data (Wang et al., 2024b). Beyond executing tasks, researchers are creating benchmarks to evaluate more subtle human-like and social behaviors. The IN3 benchmark focuses on assessing an agent’s capacity to understand user intentions by prompting them to ask clarifying questions (Qian et al., 2024). To examine the limits of agent reasoning, the OEDD corpus presents scenarios where agents must make sense of various experiences while ignoring misleading informa­ tion (George et al., 2024). Assessing collaborative and social intelligence is another critical area. SOTOPIA-π features an interactive learning approach along with an evaluation suite, SOTOPIA-EVAL, which employs both human and LLM-based assessments on aspects like goal completion and believability (Wang et al., 2024d). Additionally, frameworks have been developed to create “societies” of LLM agents to observe collaborative behaviors on tasks from the MMLU, MATH, and Chess datasets. The ability for agents to mimic human behavior is tested in frameworks that use Trust Games to compare agent decisions with recognized human patterns. Several meta-evaluation frameworks have been created to consolidate and analyze agent performance across various tasks. AgentBoard (Chang et al., 2024) offers an evaluation board that includes nine different multi-turn, partially observable tasks from areas like embodied AI, gaming, and web navigation. It provides a detailed metric to track progress, offering deeper insights beyond basic success rates. In the medical field, new benchmarks are emerging to ensure clinical safety and effectiveness. TRIAGE AGENT (Lu et al., 2024) released the first public benchmark for clinical triage, using metrics like discordance and undertriage rates against human expert performance. Other studies assess agents in their ability to execute clinical calculations using established medical calculators or make com­ plex oncology decisions based on multimodal patient data (Goodell et al., 2025; Ferber et al., 2025). These interactive benchmarks are essential for fostering the growth of more capable, reliable, and aligned LLM agents. 9.2  Methodologies and metrics for evaluation The evaluation of LLM-based agents is quickly changing from basic accuracy checks to more complex methods that look at task performance, reasoning quality, and interaction dynamics (Wang et al., 2024d; Li et al., 2023b; Chang et al., 2024). A key approach contin­ ues to focus on task-oriented performance metrics, where we measure an agent’s success by its ability to reach specific goals (Lu et al., 2024; Qin et al., 2024). 1 3 71

This is often assessed through accuracy or success rates on established benchmarks for coding, like HumanEval, math reasoning datasets such as GSM8K and MATH, and embod­ ied AI tasks in settings such as ALFRED and Overcooked-AI (Cheng et al., 2024b; Ma et al., 2024; Song et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2024b). In addition to these general benchmarks, evaluations are frequently customized for specific fields, using metrics like discordance and undertriage rates in clinical triage, the emergence of macroeconomic laws in economic sim­ ulations, and improvements in material properties for scientific discovery (Goodell et al., 2025; Ferber et al., 2025; Li et al., 2024a). For tasks where success is more subjective or quality has shades of meaning, researchers are turning to human experts and "LLM-as-a-Judge" frameworks. This approach is essential for evaluating things like the quality of travel plans, the realism and empathy of synthetic medical dialogues, and the solution quality for complex tool-use instructions. Metrics in this area often involve comparative judgments, such as win/tie/lose rates against baseline models or preference rates where evaluators choose the better of two outputs. Frameworks like SOTOPIA-EVAL use both human and LLM-based judgments across various dimen­ sions, including believability and relationship development, to evaluate social intelligence (Wang et al., 2024d). Evaluating multi-agent systems brings in metrics that capture the complexities of team­ work, social dynamics, and system-level properties (Ni and Buehler, 2024; Wang et al., 2024d). Performance is often measured by team scores, completion times, and comparisons between collaborative groups and solo agents (Zhang et al., 2024e; Cheng et al., 2024b). Methods also explore emerging social behaviors, such as conformity and reaching consen­ sus in agent societies, or the ability to simulate human trust behaviors in economic games (Zhang et al., 2024a; Li et al., 2024a). The resilience of these systems is another major con­ cern, with some evaluations measuring how performance degrades when faulty or malicious agents join the collaborative process (tse Huang et al., 2025). In addition to these outcomes, a growing number of studies focus on the efficiency and internal reasoning processes of agents. Metrics like token consumption, tool invocation effi­ ciency, and the balance between cost and quality are used to evaluate how resourceful agent solutions are (Yuan et al., 2025; Klein et al., 2025). At the same time, new methods are being developed to investigate the quality of an agent’s reasoning. This includes detailed detection of different types of errors in math problems, assessing ToM accuracy in cooperative games, and evaluating the logical coherence of reasoning sequences using formal graphs (Li et al., 2023b; Jo et al., 2023). This attention to internal processes is vital for creating more reliable and interpretable agents. To create a standard evaluation across different tasks, several meta-evaluation frame­ works have been proposed. AgentBoard (Chang et al., 2024) provides a comprehensive evaluation platform that combines nine unique multiturn tasks and introduces a detailed progress rate metric for deeper insight beyond simple success rates. Likewise, specialized evaluators like ToolEval (Qin et al., 2024) have been created to specifically assess tool- use capabilities, measuring metrics like pass rates and solution quality across thousands of real-world APIs. These initiatives indicate a maturation in the field, moving toward more comprehensive and insightful assessment tools that can help develop more capable and aligned agents. 1 3 71

These datasets are rapidly changing, moving away from traditional static text collections to dynamic, interactive, and domain-specific resources. This shift helps agents acquire complex skills and emphasizes grounding their abilities in real-world tasks, tools, and social contexts. A key strategy involves using and adapting existing public benchmarks to build core reasoning and instruction-following skills. Datasets like those for mathematics (GSM8K, MATH), question-answering (HotPotQA, StrategyQA), and coding (HumanEval) are commonly used for fine-tuning models and serve as a baseline for assessing logical and problem-solving abilities (Shinn et  al., 2023; Yin et  al., 2024; tse  Huang et  al., 2025). Instruction-tuning datasets, such as Alpaca, are used to improve the overall capabilities of models before tailoring them for specific agent tasks (Zhou et al., 2024). To promote broader agent learning, there are ongoing efforts to collect large-scale, unified annotations based on various reasoning frameworks across these complex interactive tasks. A notable trend involves employing agents to automate the enhancement and diversification of these instructional datasets, creating a constant cycle to improve data quality. A major development in agent training is creating datasets and simulated environments designed for tool use and interaction in complex digital spaces. ToolBench provides an extensive instruction-tuning dataset with over 16,000 real-world APIs, allowing models to learn to execute advanced instructions and adapt to new tools (Yang et al., 2024b). For grounding in interactive settings, benchmarks like WebShop and ALFRED serve as estab­ lished bases for training and testing web navigation and embodied instruction-following, respectively (Klein et al., 2025; Song et al., 2023). More intricate environments, such as AndroidArena (Xing et al., 2024), assess agents on complex tasks that require cooperation between applications, while TIME-ARENA (Zhang et al., 2024e) introduces time dynamics and multitasking challenges in simulated household and lab scenarios. AgentBoard (Chang et al., 2024) combines nine distinct multi-turn, partially observable tasks from areas like embodied AI, gaming, and web navigation into one evaluation framework. To ground agents in specialized, high-stakes fields, researchers are curating and gener­ ating domain-specific datasets. In the medical sector, this includes datasets derived from clinical triage manuals (TRIAGE AGENT), public EHR data such as MIMIC-IV, patient engagement logs, and extensive cancer proteomics resources such as TCGA and CCLE (Lu et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025b; Liu et al., 2025a). Benchmarks and datasets play a crucial role in evaluating LLM-based agents by directly testing key capabilities such as reasoning, planning, tool use, collaboration, and general­ ization. For reasoning, the GSM8K dataset evaluates mathematical problem-solving. The CORY framework (Ma et al., 2024) improves policy optimality by reducing distribution collapse, showing strong deductive reasoning. Similarly, HumanEval and MBPP (Bai et al., 2025) test code generation. In terms of planning, ALFRED (Song et al., 2023) assesses agents few-shot performance. LLM-Planner’s few-shot performance reveals grounding challenges. Similarly, TIME- ARENA (Zhang et al., 2024e) examines time-aware multitasking in cooking and lab tasks and highlights LLMs’ difficulties with temporal dependencies. AGENTVERSE (Cheng et al., 2024b) evaluates text understanding and coding, showing emerging cooperative behaviors. SOTOPIA-π (Wang et al., 2024d) uses MMLU to achieve social goal completion, matching GPT-4, which emphasizes social intelligence. Tool use is assessed through ToolBench (Qin et al., 2024), which tests API handling with strong zero- shot generalization. RE-Bench (Wijk et al., 2025) shows that LLMs outperform human experts in time-constrained R&D tasks, indicating effective decision-making. Multimodal grounding is evaluated through VQAv2 and Text-VQA. CogAgent (Hong et al., 2024) excels in GUI navigation, which evaluates agents’ visual-language integration. By directly examining the strengths of LLM, these benchmarks also uncover limitations, such as long-term focus issues (Zhang et al., 2024c) and social biases (Liu et al., 2025b). Although datasets in LLM-based autonomous agent research have significantly advanced areas such as reinforcement learning, code generation, healthcare, and urban planning, they still present major limitations that hinder generalization and real-world applicability. Many existing datasets are built within simulated or synthetic environments, including ALFRED (Song et al., 2023), Overcooked AI (Zhang et al., 2024b), and Sociodojo (Cheng and Chin, 2024c). These settings often fail to capture the inherent noise, unpredictability, and multi­ modal complexity of real environments, leading to overfitting and poor performance (Xing et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024d; Qiao et al., 2024). Robotics and navigation datasets, for instance Street View (Schumann et al., 2024) and AndroidArena (Xing et al., 2024) often lack diversity in user behavior, scene variation, and environmental dynamics, resulting in biased models with limited robustness (Singh et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2024c). Standard benchmarks, including HumanEval, MBPP, GSM8K, MATH, and WebShop, remain task- specific with limited cross-domain and multilingual coverage (Shinn et al., 2023; Bai et al., 2025; Ma et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024c). Existing benchmarks and datasets inadequately measure agentic reasoning by testing performance in simplified, static environments that fail to reflect real-world complexity. They often prioritize subjective, language-level evaluation over assessing an agent’s objec­ tive, action-level impact on achieving goals (Li et al., 2025a). This reliance on metrics like final success rate offers few insights into the actual reasoning process (Chang et al., 2024) and neglects crucial challenges like navigating dynamic action spaces (Xing et al., 2024). Furthermore, these benchmarks often overlook critical real-world constraints, such as tem­ poral dynamics, which are essential for assessing an agent’s ability to plan and multitask efficiently (Zhang et al., 2024e). 1 3 71

From language to action: a review of large language models as… 10  Discussion Our review explored the rapid use of LLMs as agents and tools for complex autonomous tasks. This study presents a comprehensive examination of existing LLM-based frameworks and discusses cognitive and operational components critical to agentic intelligence. By ana­ lyzing a broad spectrum of prior work, we identified how these systems are architected, the capabilities that underpin their autonomy, and the current limitations constraining their scal­ ability. We categorized the most widely adopted methods and their implementation within single-agent and multi-agent systems across various application domains. In general, this review offers a coherent foundation for understanding the developmental trajectory of LLM agents and tools to guide future advancements in this rapidly evolving field. Baseline LLMs. Recent studies addressing (RQ1) reveal that GPT-4 is currently the dom­ inant foundational model, cited in fifty-five studies, followed by GPT−3.5 in 23 studies, establishing it as a performance benchmark despite cost and access restrictions. GPT vari­ ants fulfill three roles: first, as gold-standard ablation references; second, as multi-agent col­ laborators with open models; and third, as primary reasoning modules within agent stacks. In addition to OpenAI models, Anthropic’s Claude 3 series is a prominent proprietary alternative (Zhang et al., 2024c; Chang et al., 2024; Kannan et al., 2024a; Zhang et al., 2024f). Google’s Gemini excels at very-long-context reasoning for document-scale plan­ ning. Meanwhile, the open-source ecosystem is rapidly advancing, reducing the perfor­ mance gap. Models such as LLaMA-2/3 (Zhang et al., 2024d; Zheng et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2024a; Xie et al., 2024; Ning and Liu, 2024), Mistral (Jin and Ma, 2024; Zhang et al., 2024e; Qian et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024d; Abdaljalil et al., 2025; Qiao et al., 2024; Zhai et al., 2024), Gemini (Zhang et al., 2024f; Barra et al., 2025), Qwen, DeepSeek, Vicuna, Wiz­ ardLM, and GLM-4 are increasingly adopted for coding, planning, and dialogue. Special­ ized derivatives like CodeLLaMA and ToolLLaMA demonstrate, task-specific pre-training can produce domain expertise without complete retraining. For constrained environments, Phi-2, Phi−3.5 Mini (Li et  al., 2025b), Gemini-2B, and Mistral-7B, are more efficient. Lastly, multimodality through CLIP, Stable Diffusion XL, and VQ-GAN enables LLM agents beyond text to vision and interface automation. External tool integration in LLMs. We found that integrating external tools (RQ2) is a primary driver of LLM autonomy. LLMs paired with rich computational resources, web APIs, knowledge graphs, code execution, RESTful service libraries (Qin et al., 2024), and high-fidelity simulators elevate agent capability. Real-time data retrieval from domain-spe­ cific sources strengthens RAG accuracy while speech recognition tools, such as Speechly, enable real-world interaction. Furthermore, environments such as AI2-THOR, ALFWorld, and SMAC, connected through platforms like ROS 2 and Gazebo, demonstrate that LLMs can perceive state, reason, and act in dynamic and interactive settings (Wang et al., 2023a; Shinn et al., 2023; Li et al., 2025b; Zhou et al., 2024; Frering et al., 2025). Collectively, these patterns strongly suggest that external tool access is an essential foundational mecha­ nism for accessing up-to-date knowledge, enabling perception, action, and reasoning in modern LLM agents. Frameworks for LLM agents. Our analysis of LLM agent frameworks (RQ3) reveals single-agent scenario is dominated by ReAct and Reflection, prioritizing streamlined rea­ soning-action integration and iterative self-improvement. ReAct’s thought-action sequences enable dynamic task adaptation, while Reflexion refines performance through memory- 1 3 71

S. S. Chowa et al. based learning and feedback (Shinn et al., 2023). These frameworks excel at tasks that require adaptability, minimal infrastructure, and self-guided correction. Multi-agent implementations favor frameworks such as AutoGen and CAMEL, effective for interaction, role differentiation, and collective planning (Wu et al., 2024b). AutoGen’s conversation programming supports asynchronous, modular communication workflows. CAMEL’s role-conditioned framework enables agents to solve tasks collaboratively through structured, multi-turn dialogues. These capabilities are critical for multistep reasoning, dis­ tributed system design, or collaborative creativity, where agents operate semi-independently while maintaining group objectives. LangChain is compatible in single and multi-agent setups with chain reasoning steps, memory access, and tool use (Huang et al., 2023; Klein et al., 2025). MetaGPT (Hong et al., 2023) integrates software engineering conventions among less prevalent frameworks, while AIDE (Wijk et al., 2025) and BDI (Frering et al., 2025) focus on interpretability and logical behaviors to enhance explainability and work in rule-constrained domains. The trend is shifting from instruction-bound architectures to adaptive, role-aware, and coordination-driven systems. The widespread use of ReAct, Reflexion, LangChain, and AutoGen indicates a convergence on reasoning, memory integration, and collaborative execution as core capacities. Reasoning, planning, and memory. Integration of reasoning, planning and memory mechanisms (RQ4) shaped the development of LLM-agents. During analysis, we found sin­ gle-agent frameworks like TOOLLLM (Qin et al., 2024), EASYTOOL (Yuan et al., 2025), and ToTh (Abdaljalil et al., 2025) emphasize autonomy, safety, and introspective capabil­ ity. In contrast, multi-agent frameworks like AGENTVERSE (Cheng et al., 2024b), Thread Memory (Jin and Ma, 2024), and ToM (Li et al., 2023b) prioritize coordination, belief mod­ eling, and contextual reasoning. AGENTVERSE implements collaborative reasoning using structured symbolic modules; Thread Memory preserves context in multi-turn dialogue and interaction; ToM enhances coordination by modeling belief states in multi-agent settings. CoT, ReAct, and Self-Reflection appear in both. CoT is effective in code generation and robotics (Bai et al., 2025; Li et al., 2023b), where ReAct (Zhang et al., 2024e; Singh et al., 2024) and Reflexion (Zhang et al., 2024e; Feng et al., 2024) integrate feedback-aware rea­ soning, contributing to real-time adaptability and iterative self-improvement. Single agent planning strategies, such as ReHAC (Feng et al., 2024) and RAFA (Liu et  al., 2024a), emphasize proactive multistep forecasting and heuristic goal decomposi­ tion. Multi-agent systems such as DeCoAgent (Jin et al., 2024) and SMART-LLM (Kan­ nan et al., 2024a) address coordination through prompt-based decomposition and coalition formation, respectively. In particular, adaptive and evolution-based planning in Star-Agents (Zhou et al., 2024) and UrbanKGent (Ning and Liu, 2024) reflect increasing interest in long- horizon self-organizing workflows. We observe a clear divide between localized and distributed memory. Single-agent mod­ els optimize within episode retention using episodic reprompting (Zheng et al., 2024), com­ pressed logs (Huang et al., 2023), or symbolic graphs (Abdaljalil et al., 2025), supporting isolated task continuity. Multi-agent models like ProAgent (Zhang et al., 2024b) provide shared task memory and thread-level history, while MATRIX (Pang et al., 2024) gener­ ates diverse interaction data as a multi-agent simulation environment, rather than managing shared memory. Context windows (Zhang et al., 2023; Pang et al., 2024) and dialogue his­ tory (Wang et al., 2024d; Li et al., 2023a) underpin both categories, while hybrid memory 1 3 71

From language to action: a review of large language models as… systems (Boiko et al., 2023; Gao et al., 2024) signal convergence toward unified architec­ tures that bridge short/long-term retention. Prompting, fine-tuning, and memory augmentation. Our findings showed that agent autonomy is enabled by prompt engineering, fine-tuning, and memory augmentation (RQ5). Prompt engineering, a non-parametric technique, allows flexible, inference-time control over agent behavior, as seen in MechAgents (Ni and Buehler, 2024) and AGENTVERSE (Cheng et al., 2024b), which used structured prompts to simulate complex interactions such as expert collaboration, role play, trust modeling, and cognitive biases. However, in special domains where prompting is insufficient, fine-tuning is employed as a parametric approach to internalize domain expertise and task-specific skills, as seen in ToolLLM (Qin et al., 2024) for tool use specialization, RISE for self-correction abilities, and SOTOPIA-π (Wang et al., 2024d) for modeling social intelligence. Likewise, memory augmentation through external RAG and internal episodic memory is essential to ground agents in real-world contexts and support long-term reasoning. For example, TRIAGEAGENT (Lu et al., 2024) utilizes medical knowledge retrieval to mitigate hallucination, while Reflexion (Shinn et al., 2023) enables agents to adapt based on accumulated experience. Therefore, the architectural and behavioral autonomy of modern LLM agents is largely scaffolded by design choices rather than innate model capabilities. Evaluation and benchmarks. Our analysis indicated that evaluating LLM-based agents (RQ6) requires a methodological change, from static NLP benchmarks to dynamic process- oriented evaluations. We also found that a robust evaluation framework should incorpo­ rate final outputs and the full agentic process. For example, AGENTBOARD (Chang et al., 2024) introduces "progress rate" metrics that capture incremental task completion across intermediate steps. Similarly, RE-Bench (Wijk et al., 2025) aligns agent performance with human expert benchmarks on complex research problems, reinforcing the importance of human-level baselines in agent evaluation. In addition to this, controlled simulations reveal handling unreliable or adversarial col­ laborators (tse Huang et al., 2025), highlighting resilience as a critical component of agent intelligence. Domain-specific evaluations also emerged as essential for assessing practical­ ity. For example, ChemCrow (Bran et al., 2024) benchmarks autonomous chemical synthe­ sis against metrics grounded in scientific outputs, while tool-integrated agents in healthcare significantly reduce clinical calculation errors (Goodell et al., 2025). Our analysis points to the growing recognition of failure analysis and safety evaluations as a key to agent benchmarking. Adversarial testing techniques are being developed to expose vulnerabilities, including backdoor attacks (Yang et al., 2024b), while new approaches such as PrivacyAsst (Zhang et al., 2024f) aim to maintain data confidentiality and trustworthiness during agent deployment. The evaluation state for LLM agents is rapidly evolving towards more comprehensive, interactive, and context-aware approaches. These emerging strategies emphasize whether an agent can succeed and how it reasons, interacts, adapts, and safe­ guards users along the way. 1 3 71

To build agents that are reliable, adaptive, and ethically aligned, challenges such as unverifiable reasoning, limited contextual collaboration, vulnerability to adversarial attacks, and inadequate person­ alization must be addressed. In this section, we outline the key areas where future work and critical research is needed (RQ7). Table S3, in the Supplementary Material, provides an organized summary of the existing research gaps and potential research pathways discussed in this section. 11.1  Towards verifiable reasoning and robust self-improvement Although current agents based on LLMs show impressive abilities, their reasoning pro­ cesses frequently remain unclear, and their capacity to learn from failure is limited. This lack of clarity and inflexibility limits their usage. Future work should develop agents with clear, verifiable reasoning methods and strong, efficient self-improvement cycles. One major trend in improving reasoning is shifting from unstructured, free-form "CoT" to more organized and logically sound frameworks. Some methods ensure logical consis­ tency from the start. For example, the ToTh model’s reasoning is a multi-agent collabora­ tion that simulates abductive, deductive, and inductive inference, assembling outputs into a formal reasoning graph, validating for coherence (Abdaljalil et al., 2025). In future works, a similar approach could assist in detecting financial fraud or security breaches by produc­ ing a reasoning graph that will provide a transparent, stepwise logic trail that authorities Fig. 7  Limitations in the current landscape of LLM-based agents and corresponding mitigation strategies

From language to action: a review of large language models as… can trace and validate. MechAgents (Ni and Buehler, 2024) utilizes a team of agents for complex engineering challenges and self-correcting physics-based simulation code. This verifies the reasoning of the agent against established scientific models. Building on this strategy, future work may explore the potential drug-drug interactions by modeling their combined molecular effects. Combining LLMs with traditional symbolic AI approaches, such as Belief-Desire-Intention agents, enables verifiable decision-making and improves safety (Frering et al., 2025). An essential aspect of verifiability is identifying and addressing flaws in the reasoning process. FG-PRM research (Li et al., 2024c) reliably tackles this by creating a classification of errors in mathematical reasoning and training a reward model to identify and penalize these errors. Alongside verifiable reasoning is the goal of strong self-improvement, where agents learn from experience without needing retraining. Through strategies like Reflexion, agents can reflect on their performance and learn from mistakes, using verbal RL, creating a memory of these reflections that guides future attempts (Shinn et al., 2023). Studies such as RISE employ recursive introspection to fine-tune models through an ongoing process of self- correction, to improve their output over time (Xi et al., 2025). Subsequent work could apply these strategies to develop an agent for biomedical image segmentation that self-improves iteratively, minimizes reliance on continuous large-scale human annotation, and adapts to patient-specific image differences. Multi-agent dynamics also serves as a robust method for promoting self-improvement. In the CORY framework, a model is split into pioneer and observer agents that co-evolve through a cooperative RL process. This improves resilience and avoids policy failures common in traditional RL fine-tuning (Ma et al., 2024). Other frameworks, such as COPPER (Bo et al., 2024), feature a special reflector agent that pro­ vides tailored, constructive feedback to other agents, improving teamwork through a system­ atic self-improvement loop. Some studies, such as AgentOptimizer (Zhang et al., 2024h), suggest treating agent tools as learnable parameters, enabling task adaptation through tool improvement. Likewise, AVATAR (Wu et al., 2024) automates the optimization of prompts for tool use by employing a comparator module to reason over both positive and negative examples. Integrating structured reasoning, introspective learning, and adaptive capabilities is driving LLM agents toward more reliability, transparency, and continual improvement. 11.2  Towards scalable, adaptive, and collaborative LLM-based agent systems Future research should enhance LLM agents’ scalability, adaptability, and real-time opera­ tional capacity, for deployment in multimodal and domain-specific environments (Wang et al., 2025b; Yang et al., 2024a; Zeng et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025c). Beyond internal agent reasoning and learning mechanisms, future work should address infrastructure con­ straints, memory usage, and latency, while enabling efficient inference through architectural techniques such as KV caching and optimized decoders (Jin and Ma, 2024; Zeng et al., 2024). These improvements are vital for low-resource or time-sensitive scenarios, such as on-device processing or streaming interaction. Another key priority lies in enhancing multi-agent collaboration and the development of perceptually aware communication. The absence of adaptive communication protocols and contextual modeling in frameworks such as AGENTVERSE (Cheng et al., 2024b) limits their ability in dynamic multi-agent environments (Wijk et al., 2025). Future agent systems should adopt human-inspired, socially grounded dialogue strategies to enhance collabora­ 1 3 71

S. S. Chowa et al. tion capability, contextual awareness and intent inference among agents (Kim et al., 2024). Such improvements will enable the deployment of lightweight agents on edge hardware for traffic systems, warehouses, and drones, facilitating inter-agent communication and collaboration. Furthermore, as the range of agent applications expands, extending to gesture-based interfaces, EHR prediction, collaborative games, continuous learning, coevolutionary train­ ing, and prompt refinement methods become essential (Wang et al., 2025b). Simultane­ ously, development of negotiation-heavy simulations like Lewis-style coordination games or Diplomacy can facilitate deeper understanding of agent reasoning under critical settings (Wijk et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2024d). Likewise, ensuring robustness and interpretability remains a primary concern. Beyond introspective reasoning and verification, transparent evaluation pipelines are needed to track agent behavior over time, particularly under unpredictability and emergence. The accel­ eration of open-source advancements, led by models such as LLaMA-2-70B, provides an accessible, scalable, reproducible foundation, enabling researchers to collectively develop safe, effective, socially aligned agentic systems (Li et al., 2025a; Yin et al., 2024). 11.3  Deepening the human-agent symbiosis: personalization, proactivity, and trust Future research should enhance autonomy, alignment, and practical deployability of LLM- based agents, for complex, dynamic, open-ended, and high-stakes environments. Increased operational freedom produces emergent effects, from strategic cooperative gains to unsafe shortcut-seeking actions. Addressing this duality requires robust alignment strategies to mitigate adverse behaviors while preserving constructive autonomy to operate efficiently and effectively. Simultaneously, the strategic focus is shifting toward human-centered augmentation, emphasizing collaboration, reliability, and personalization. Realizing this calls for advances in intent recognition and co-creative interaction, where agents can engage in context-sensi­ tive conversations that anticipate user needs and refine task goals interactively, an approach illustrated by studies like "Tell Me More" (Qian et al., 2024) and ReHAC (Feng et al., 2024). Long-term personalization represents a critical research frontier in which future agents should build persistent, evolving user models over time while addressing memory and pri­ vacy, as stated in studies like PrivacyAsst (Zhang et al., 2024f). Achieving such personal­ ization requires integrating multimodal capabilities while aligning interface modalities to user-specific preferences. Recently, personalized LLM-based agents have introduced com­ plex ethical and societal risks, anthropomorphism, and over-trust. Their humanlike interac­ tions create deception and encourage vulnerable populations, such as children or the elderly, to disclose sensitive information (Peter et al., 2025). Since LLM-based agents lack moral agency, attributing accountability is conceptually flawed (Meier, 2025). Beyond interface risks, agent architectures suffer from jailbreaking (Shen et al., 2024), and environmental signal-triggered backdoor attacks (Yang et  al., 2024b). Jailbreaking refers to deliberate overriding of built-in safety measures of LLMs (Ouyang et al., 2022), and since agents need to handle multi-round dialogues and multiple sources of information, they become more prone to jailbreaking attacks. Effective human-agent collaboration requires both resilient 1 3 71

Continuous model optimization across collaborative decoding, lightweight modular execution strategies, and efficient caching mechanisms drives real-world scalability and enables a new class of agents that go beyond technical proficiency to ethically aligned, emo­ tionally aware, privacy-conscious, and deeply integrated in complex workflows. 12  Conclusion In this article, we present a comprehensive overview of LLM-based agents and the inte­ gration of tools within these systems. We examined how prompt engineering, fine-tuning, memory enhancement, and tool use contribute to the building of LLM agents by address­ ing seven focused research questions. We observed that single-agent systems prioritize autonomy and introspective decision making. However, multi-agent systems focus on coor­ dination, role distribution, and collaborative planning. Crucially, this distinction becomes domain sensitive, with multi-agent configurations demonstrating pronounced advantages in areas requiring social intelligence, cooperative problem solving, and high-stakes decision support, such as healthcare, scientific research, and complex engineering tasks. Integrat­ ing external tools, real-time data sources, and multimodal systems has become essential to enable LLM agents to perform tasks beyond the limitations of pre-trained models. In paral­ lel, the evaluation of these agents is changing from static accuracy-based benchmarks to dynamic process-oriented methods that account for reasoning quality, adaptability, and task completion in real-world settings. We have also examined critical limitations and safety concerns as LLM agents are deployed in sensitive environments. These include risks related to security, performance limitations, adaptability in dynamic or personalized settings, and challenges in trust, explainability, and agent co-evolution. Addressing these challenges will ensure reliability, trust, and efficiency in future applications. In our view, future work should focus on two critical goals: making agent reasoning transparent and verifiable and developing reliable methods for self-improvement without compromising safety. These capabilities are critical in high-risk environments, where errors can have serious consequences. Ensuring that LLM agents are trustworthy, resilient, and aligned with domain-specific requirements will be central to their responsible deployment across disciplines. Beyond Topic Modeling: Comparative Evaluation of Topic Interpretation by Large Language Models Tiago de Melo1 and Paolo Merialdo2 1 State University of Amazonas, Amazonas, Brazil 2 Roma Tre University, Rome, Italy tmelo@uea.edu.br, paolo.merialdo@uniroma3.it Abstract. This study investigates the application of Large Language Models (LLMs) for interpreting topics derived from topic modeling within the domain of restaurant reviews in Brazilian Portuguese. Traditional topic modeling techniques often produce outputs that require further in- terpretation to fully capture the nuanced meanings within the data. This research leverages the advanced natural language processing capabilities of LLMs to provide deeper insights into these topics, aiming to bridge the gap between computational topic identification and human-like un- derstanding. A comparative analysis of several LLMs, including Chat- GPT versions 3.5 and 4.0 and Google’s BARD, was conducted to assess their efficacy in interpreting the generated topics from a large dataset of restaurant reviews. The topics identified were subjected to interpretation by both human evaluators and LLMs, enabling a direct comparison be- tween human and machine-generated interpretations. Preliminary results indicate that LLMs, especially with well-crafted prompts, can produce interpretations that are closely aligned with human understanding, un- derscoring their potential utility in qualitative data analysis within NLP applications. This research not only sheds light on the interpretative ca- pabilities of LLMs but also opens new pathways for automating complex interpretive tasks across diverse linguistic and cultural landscapes. Keywords: Large language model, Natural language processing, Topic models 1 Introduction Unsupervised learning aims to extract information from unlabeled data. Topic modeling, a technique in Natural Language Processing (NLP), is particularly designed for this task and has been applied across various domains, including online reviews analysis [1], recommendation systems [2], and healthcare [3]. Several metrics, such as topic coherence, perplexity, and diversity, are used to evaluate the quality of the generated topics [4]. However, these metrics do not provide insights into why an item belongs to a particular topic or the labeling of each topic. While human evaluation is considered the gold standard in NLP,

2 Tiago de Melo et al. it is often laborious, expensive, and time-consuming. For instance, Rijcken et al. [5] analyzed 3,210 topic models and relied on coherence metrics for evaluation, noting that human assessment would be ideal but impractical due to the sheer volume of topics generated by the trained models. Therefore, an important task following topic identification is their interpretation [6], aiming to understand the prominent features within each topic. Efforts in the literature have been made to make unsupervised learning tech- niques explainable, through inherently explainable methods [7, 8] and concepts from eXplainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) [9, 10]. However, these approaches are often algorithm or model-dependent and do not typically produce user- friendly descriptions of topic interpretations that can be easily understood by non-technical audiences, such as business and marketing professionals who are often the primary stakeholders in unlabeled outcomes. With the advent of Large Language Models (LLMs) that generate increas- ingly human-like responses [3], this paper proposes investigating the use of gener- ative languages as a substitute for human intervention in the task of interpreting generated topics by topic modellings. Our hypothesis is that it will be possible to replace human assessment in the task of topic interpretation. Despite significant advancements in LLMs, there is, to our knowledge, no prior work focused on the interpretability of topic models for automatic evaluation. In order to validate our hypothesis, we evaluate and compare the perfor- mance of three publicly available LLMs: OpenAI’s ChatGPT-3.5 and GPT-4.0, and Google’s Bard, in the task of interpreting topics generated by well-known models in the literature. We applied a set of widely recognized topic identification methods to a large corpus of web-published restaurant reviews in Portuguese. The choice of restaurant reviews is motivated by the volume and diversity of data they generate, rich in opinions, sentiments, and varied experiences. Furthermore, Brazilian Portuguese, as a language of analysis, presents unique linguistic and cultural challenges due to its rich variation [11]. We also assess the importance of prompts and how these models’ outcomes compare to human analysis. Interpretable Topic Models 3 2 Related Work 2.1 Topic Modeling Algorithms Topic modeling algorithms in natural language processing are unsupervised tech- niques designed to identify semantic coherence within large datasets by analyzing the likelihood of words belonging to specific topics. These algorithms, such as Fuzzy Latent Semantic Analysis (FLSA), Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA), and BertTopic, employ various strategies to reduce data dimensionality and enhance interpretability. Fuzzy Latent Semantic Analysis (FLSA). FLSA, building upon the foun- dation laid by LSA, utilizes singular value decomposition (SVD) to uncover latent semantic structures, further incorporating fuzzy logic to refine semantic interpretation (Karami et al., 2018). By applying fuzzy c-means clustering and leveraging Bayes’ theorem and linear algebra, FLSA enhances the granularity of topic detection and interpretation, marking a significant advancement in the nuanced analysis of textual content (Bezdek, 2013). Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA). Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) is a pivotal advancement in the domain of topic modeling, predicated on the princi- ple that documents can be represented as mixtures of multiple topics, wherein each topic is defined by a distinct distribution of words. This generative model assumes that documents are composed of latent topics, and these topics are in turn composed of a set of words, allowing for a layered decomposition of textual data [12]. LDA employs a probabilistic approach, utilizing Dirichlet distributions to model the variability in topic distributions across documents and the word distributions within topics. This framework enables the extraction of a set of topics that best represent the underlying thematic structures in a large corpus of text, providing a robust method for uncovering hidden semantic patterns. The strength of LDA lies in its ability to handle large volumes of text data, making it an indispensable tool for uncovering the thematic essence of extensive text collections and facilitating a deeper analytical insight into the corpus’ content. BertTopic. BERTopic advances the field by integrating BERT embeddings with a cluster-based TF-IDF approach, efficiently extracting dense topic clus- ters through dimensionality reduction via the unified manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) technique [13]. This method’s ability to identify the most representative terms for each topic makes it particularly suitable for di- verse applications, especially in scenarios where the range of topics is vast and undefined. These algorithms collectively demonstrate the evolution of topic modeling techniques, from foundational methods like LDA to more advanced approaches such as BERTopic, each contributing uniquely to the field’s understanding and capability in extracting meaningful topics from extensive textual data.

4 Tiago de Melo et al. 2.2 Large Language Models Recent advancements in generative language models have opened new avenues for topic interpretation and analysis. Notably, models like ChatGPT 3.5 and ChatGPT 4, developed by OpenAI, along with Google’s BARD, represent sig- nificant milestones in the field of Natural Language Processing (NLP), showcas- ing advanced capabilities in text comprehension and generation that approach human-like fluency. ChatGPT 3.5 and ChatGPT 4. ChatGPT 3.5 and ChatGPT 4 are part of the GPT (Generative Pre-trained Transformer) model family, which are trained on a wide array of internet text, enabling them to generate coherent and contex- tually relevant text in response to diverse prompts. The key difference between the versions lies in their scale and comprehension ability, with ChatGPT 4 of- fering significant improvements in terms of accuracy, responsiveness to more complex contexts, and sensitivity to linguistic and cultural nuances. BARD. On the other hand, Google’s BARD is designed to provide informative and contextually rich responses, utilizing the Transformer-based language model architecture to process and generate text. While specific details on BARD’s im- plementation and training might be less disclosed, its objective aligns with that of GPT models: to produce text that is relevant, informative, and linguistically coherent. The application of these generative language models in the context of topic interpretation is particularly promising. They offer the potential to automate and enrich qualitative analysis of textual data, providing insights that extend beyond mere identification of keywords or phrases representative of topics. Through the generation of summaries, explanations, or even interactive dialogues, these models can facilitate a deeper understanding of the underlying themes in large text datasets, without the need for extensive human intervention. However, applying these advanced models to topic interpretation is not with- out challenges. Issues such as embedded bias, reliability of the generated inter- pretations, and the ability to adapt to domain-specific contexts are active areas of research. This study seeks to explore the potential of generative language models, including ChatGPT 3.5, ChatGPT 4, and BARD, in the automatic in- terpretation of topics, assessing their effectiveness compared to human analysis and contributing to the understanding of how these technologies can be effec- tively applied in text analysis. 3 Methodology We proposed a framework for topic interpretation and analysis. The framework is shown in Fig. 2. It is a three-step procedure that includes: (1) topic identification, (2) topic interpretation, and (3) topic evaluation.

Framework for topic interpretation and analysis 3.1 Dataset In this study, we developed a Python crawler to gather user reviews posted in Brazilian Portuguese on two popular online review platforms: Google Reviews1 and TripAdvisor2. We successfully collected 100,000 restaurant reviews in Brazil- ian Portuguese, spanning from 1996 to 2023. Opinion Themes. User reviews were divided into sentences, and we assumed that these sentences are linked to a pre-defined set of themes, based on other re- search [14, 15] for theme definition. Sentences were categorized into the following themes: ambiance, drinks, food, general, location, price, and service. Sentences related to decoration, interior, music, space, lighting, or capacity were classified as ambiance. Sentences about beer, wine, or beverages were classified as drinks. Sentences related to food, desserts, menu, or dishes were classified as food. Sen- tences about transportation or access to the restaurant were classified as location. Sentences regarding the cost of the service or restaurant products were classified as price. Sentences related to staff attitudes, efficiency, interaction with the man- ager, or delays were classified as service. Sentences about the restaurant itself, such as “excellent restaurant”, were classified as general. Finally, we decided to discard sentences that did not fit into any of the above themes so that we could control the classification of topics by the methods. 1 http://business.google.com 2 https://www.tripadvisor.com.br

A second evaluator reviewed the annotated sentences and discarded those with classification discrepancies. These sentences were replaced with others from the same theme to ensure each theme had an equal number of sentences. The fi- nal dataset3 consisted of 21,000 sentences, evenly distributed across the seven themes. 3.2 Preprocessing To guarantee that the topics derived accurately represent the underlying theme of the corpus, it is necessary to eliminate words that are frequently used but carry little informational value. These are words that do not provide relevant in- formation about the document’s content. Initially, all sentences were converted to lowercase to standardize the analysis. This was followed by the removal of empty strings, punctuations, and excessive whitespace, which helps in eliminat- ing unnecessary noise in the text. After this step, the sentences were transformed into word lists. The next critical step was the removal of stopwords - common words that frequently appear in language but do not significantly contribute to the specific meaning of the sentences, such as prepositions, articles, and con- junctions. Removing these words is crucial to focus on the words that truly contribute to identifying the latent themes in the corpus. 3.3 Topic Identification In the field of Natural Language Processing (NLP), topic modeling is an essential method for uncovering hidden thematic structures within large text corpora. This technique is instrumental in organizing, understanding, and summarizing vast datasets of textual information. Topic modeling involves the identification of topics, which are sets of words that frequently occur together, revealing the underlying themes present in a collection of documents. Among the various topic modeling algorithms, Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) [16], Factorized Latent Semantic Analysis (FLSA) [17], and BERTopic [13] have gained prominence. LDA, a generative probabilistic model, assumes doc- uments are mixtures of topics and topics are mixtures of words. This allows for the discovery of topics that are represented as a distribution over words. FLSA, on the other hand, is a matrix factorization technique that decomposes the term-document matrix into two lower-dimensional matrices, capturing the latent structures in the data. BERTopic leverages the power of BERT embed- dings, a cutting-edge transformer model, to create dense clusters of semantically similar text, leading to more nuanced and contextually rich topic extraction. We also experimented to generate topics using ChatGPT, an advanced language model. ChatGPT’s ability to understand and generate human-like text offered a unique perspective in topic modeling, potentially enhancing the quality and relevance of the extracted topics. 3 https://data.mendeley.com/datasets/p4mfcpjkyp/1

Interpretable Topic Models 7 Metrics to Evaluate Models. In order to evaluate the topic models, we em- ployed the coherence score (Cv) to quantify this. Topic coherence is typically defined as the mean semantic relatedness among the most probable words in a topic, as cited in literature [18]. This concept originates from the distribu- tional hypothesis in linguistics, which posits that words sharing similar mean- ings often appear in comparable contexts. Among various coherence measures, Cv has been found to correlate most closely with human assessments of topic relevance [19]. Consequently, this study adopts the Cv metric for evaluation, aligning with methodologies employed in prior research [17]. The Cv measure involves calculating the co-occurrence frequencies of words within a specified context window. These frequencies are then utilized to compute the normalized point-wise mutual information for each word pair, culminating in unique vec- tors for each word. The topic coherence score, derived from the average cosine similarities between each word’s vector and the aggregate of all word vectors, is quantified by the Cv metric [20]. This score, ranging from zero to one, indicates the degree of coherence within the topic model, with one representing perfect coherence and zero indicating a lack of coherence. This metric is pivotal in eval- uating the effectiveness and interpretability of topic models in natural language processing. 3.4 Topic Interpretation Human Interpretation. After selecting the most coherent set of topics, we asked a group of people and various generative languages to interpret the gen- erated topics. Each topic was represented by a set of 10 words, each with its respective probability of belonging to that topic. We requested that individuals evaluate the topics and categorize each one under one of the themes described in Section 3.1. If the topic was about restau- rants but did not fit any of the predetermined themes, it should be marked as “other”. Finally, if the topic was outside the restaurant domain, it should be classified as “invalid”. Model Interpretation. We also asked for different large language models (LLMs) to interpret the generated topics. In this regard, we considered Chat- GPT and BARD, employing two different versions of ChatGPT, version 3.5 and version 4.0. These models were selected due to their representation of the state-of-the-art in LLM technology. We further experimented with three different prompts for the LLMs to assess the influence of prompt selection on the final outcome. The prompts are described in Table 1, where Prompt 1 provides no context, Prompt 2 informs that the topics are related to the restaurant domain, and Prompt 3 guides the LLMs on the possible expected responses. In all the prompts, examples of responses were not presented, nor was the conversation history used.

This analysis focused on identifying similarities and differences between the outcomes to assess the feasibility of utilizing a LLM for interpreting topics generated by topic modeling algorithms. Our comparative analysis involved a detailed evaluation of the degree of con- cordance between the topics identified by human evaluators and those identified by LLMs, such as ChatGPT and BARD. This examination included assessing the precision and relevance of the topics identified by each method. We consid- ered factors like thematic accuracy, context relevance, and the granularity of the topics identified. Additionally, we explored the potential of LLMs in providing insights beyond the scope of human interpretation. This included evaluating the ability of LLMs to identify nuanced subtopics or to provide a broader context to the primary topics, which might not be immediately evident to human evaluators. The results of this comparative analysis will be instrumental in determining the extent to which LLMs can be reliably used for topic interpretation in Natural Language Processing (NLP) applications. Furthermore, this study aims to shed light on the strengths and limitations of both human and machine-based topic identification, providing a comprehensive understanding of the role of LLMs in NLP. 4 Experiments 4.1 Topic Identification The models Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA), Factorized Latent Semantic Analysis (FLSA), BertTopic, and the large language model ChatGPT 4.0 were employed to discover the most pertinent topics for restaurant consumers. Follow- ing methodologies similar to those described by Syed and Spruit [21] and Ordun et al. [22], our experiments varied the number of topics from 1 to 20, selecting

Notably, the results for ChatGPT suggest its potential viability as a topic identification model. Interpretable Topic Models 13 The observed results deviate from expectations, considering that more recent language models are generally presumed to possess greater capabilities, partic- ularly given their training on larger datasets. We contemplate several potential reasons for this unexpected outcome. OpenAI consistently implements changes, yet we lack clarity on the specific process and criteria employed to evaluate whether these models are advancing or regressing. Furthermore, Chen et al. [24] have provided preliminary evidence that validates substantial fluctuations in the performance of API-served models. They uncovered significant variations in the performance of GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 across four diverse tasks within a mere three-month period (from March to June 2023). For example, GPT-4 initially exhibited an impressive 97.6% accuracy in identifying prime numbers, but by June, its accuracy had plummeted to a mere 2.4%. Conversely, GPT-3.5 dis- played an opposite trend, consistently improving over time. Interestingly, LLM models also provide explanations for topic annotations, a capability that sets them apart from human annotators who may sometimes make decisions without the ability to elucidate their choices. For instance, the ChatGPT 3.5 model with Prompt 3 explained why it chose the name for topic 7 as follows: “The list includes terms like “atendimento” (service), “ambiente” (ambiance), “comida” (food), “bom” (good), “excelente” (excellent). These terms provide a broad description of the restaurant, encompassing various aspects such as service (S), ambiance (A), and food (F). However, the presence of general terms covering multiple categories suggests that it is most suitable for catego- rization under General Restaurant (G).”. This highlights how LLMs not only have the ability to automate topic annotation but also provide insights into the reasoning behind their decisions. Regarding prompt utilization, it is evident that task performance improves with more detailed instructions for the models. Hence, the use of Prompt 3 yielded better results across all three models investigated. Notably, even in the case of Prompt 1, where the models had no prior context, they displayed a re- markable ability to annotate correctly in the majority of cases. This underscores the models’ adaptability and proficiency in topic annotation when provided with more explicit instructions. 5 Limitations A notable limitation of our study is its reliance on a specific, balanced dataset comprising predominantly restaurant user reviews. This specificity raises ques- tions about the generalizability of our findings to different domains or data distributions. Moreover, our approach to interpreting topics hinges on their co- herence, aligning with the methodology proposed in recent research by Dieng et al. [25]. However, it’s important to acknowledge that coherence may not con- sistently align with human interpretation, as indicated by Rijcken et al. [17]. Furthermore, reducing the concept of interpretability to a singular numerical value oversimplifies its complexity. Although employing a single metric, such as coherence, offers a practical means for comparing topics on a large scale, it

14 Tiago de Melo et al. should be noted that interpretability encompasses a broader range of factors and cannot be fully encapsulated by a single measure. This recognition of the multifaceted nature of interpretability is crucial in the ongoing development and evaluation of natural language processing algorithms. 6 Conclusions This paper introduced a methodology for topic interpretation leveraging large language models (LLMs). The methodology encompasses a three-step process: topic identification using a dedicated topic modeling, annotation of topics by human evaluators, and interpretation by LLMs, followed by a comparative anal- ysis. Despite the observed discrepancies between human annotations and the in- terpretations rendered by LLMs, the degree of inconsistency was found to be minimal. This suggests the feasibility of employing LLMs for what is tradi- tionally a human-centric task of topic interpretation. The influence of prompt design on the task’s outcome was also examined. Experimental results demon- strate that the ChatGPT model, particularly version 3.5, when equipped with a detailed prompt (P3), is capable of interpreting topics and yielding valuable insights. Therefore, we posit that LLMs hold significant potential for topic in- terpretation. For future work, we aim to extend the application of the proposed method- ology to additional idioms and domains. Furthermore, we plan to customize an open-source LLM to specifically cater to the task of topic interpretation. In addition, the coherence scores achieved from ChatGPT show a consistent perfor- mance, suggesting that it may serve as an effective model for the identification and interpretation of topics in large datasets. Therefore, a promising avenue for future work involves a deeper investigation into the use of ChatGPT as a topic modeling tool. Systematic Reviews Title and abstract screening for literature reviews using large language models: an exploratory study in the biomedical domain Fabio Dennstädt1,3*   , Johannes Zink2, Paul Martin Putora1,3, Janna Hastings4,5,6 and Nikola Cihoric3 Abstract Background  Systematically screening published literature to determine the relevant publications to synthesize in a review is a time-consuming and difficult task. Large language models (LLMs) are an emerging technology with promising capabilities for the automation of language-related tasks that may be useful for such a purpose. Methods  LLMs were used as part of an automated system to evaluate the relevance of publications to a certain topic based on defined criteria and based on the title and abstract of each publication. A Python script was created to generate structured prompts consisting of text strings for instruction, title, abstract, and relevant criteria to be provided to an LLM. The relevance of a publication was evaluated by the LLM on a Likert scale (low relevance to high relevance). By specifying a threshold, different classifiers for inclusion/exclusion of publications could then be defined. The approach was used with four different openly available LLMs on ten published data sets of biomedical literature reviews and on a newly human-created data set for a hypothetical new systematic literature review. Results  The performance of the classifiers varied depending on the LLM being used and on the data set ana- lyzed. Regarding sensitivity/specificity, the classifiers yielded 94.48%/31.78% for the FlanT5 model, 97.58%/19.12% for the OpenHermes-NeuralChat model, 81.93%/75.19% for the Mixtral model and 97.58%/38.34% for the Platypus 2 model on the ten published data sets. The same classifiers yielded 100% sensitivity at a specificity of 12.58%, 4.54%, 62.47%, and 24.74% on the newly created data set. Changing the standard settings of the approach (minor adaption of instruction prompt and/or changing the range of the Likert scale from 1–5 to 1–10) had a considerable impact on the performance. Conclusions  LLMs can be used to evaluate the relevance of scientific publications to a certain review topic and clas- sifiers based on such an approach show some promising results. To date, little is known about how well such systems would perform if used prospectively when conducting systematic literature reviews and what further implications this might have. However, it is likely that in the future researchers will increasingly use LLMs for evaluating and classifying scientific publications.
